en: The Nṛsiṃha-tāpinī Upaniṣad The Nṛsiṃha-uttara-tāpinī Upaniṣad
In the Nṛsiṃhottaratāpinī, the splendor consisting of the fourth of the fourth (turyaturya),
the empire of supreme non-duality, is perceived directly.

"Oṃ! The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: 'Explain to us this Self, the syllable Oṃ, which is subtler than the subtle. He said, 'So be it. This syllable 'Oṃ' is all this; its further explanation is as follows: whatever has been, whatever is, and whatever will be—all that is the syllable Oṃ alone. And whatever else transcends the three periods of time, that too is the syllable Oṃ alone. For all this is Brahman, and this Self is Brahman. Having unified this very Self with Brahman by means of 'Oṃ,' and having unified Brahman with the Self by means of 'Oṃ'—"

Having experienced that one which is undecaying, immortal, and fearless as "Om," and having superposed upon it this entire universe consisting of the three bodies—since that [universe] is indeed identical with and composed of that [Self]—one should withdraw it into that very Self with the syllable "Om. One should meditate upon this very Self, which possesses three bodies, as the Supreme Brahman, which also possesses three bodies: because of its grossness and because it experiences the gross; because of its subtlety and because it experiences the subtle; and because of its unity and because it experiences bliss. This Self has four quarters: the waking state, whose intellect is gross, which has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, which experiences the gross, and which is fourfold in nature.

The Universal (Viśva), Vaiśvānara, is the first foot. The second foot is Taijasa, Hiraṇyagarbha—the one whose sphere is the state of dream, who possesses subtle cognition, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, who experiences the subtle, and who is fourfold in nature. The third foot is Prājña, Īśvara—the state of deep sleep where, being asleep, one desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream; there he becomes unified, a mass of pure consciousness, consisting of bliss, experiencing bliss, having the mind as his gateway, and being fourfold in nature.

He is the Lord of all; He is the All-knowing; He is the Inner Controller; He is the source of all, for He is the origin and the dissolution of all beings. These three states—deep sleep, dream, and mere illusion—are also [contained within Him]. Indeed, this Self is of the nature of pure consciousness alone. Now, as for the Fourth (Turiya), which consists of four aspects: because it is established in the Fourth, each of the other three states—deep sleep, dream, and mere illusion—is here also [subsumed] through the states of the "One who permits" (Anujñātṛ), the "One who permits and observes" (Anujñā), and the "One who discriminates" (Vikalpa). Indeed, this Self is of the nature of pure consciousness alone. Now, this is the instruction: [the Self is] neither one whose cognition is gross, nor one whose cognition is subtle, nor one whose cognition is both, nor...

Indeed, this very Self is one who is awake while waking, without dreaming or deep sleep; awake while dreaming, without deep sleep; awake while in deep sleep, without dreaming; and awake in the fourth state (*turiya*), without dreaming or deep sleep, never deviating therefrom—eternally blissful, the single essence of Being. For He is indeed the seer of the eye, the seer of the ear, the seer of speech, the seer of the mind, the seer of the intellect, the seer of the vital breath, the seer of darkness, the seer of everything; therefore, He is other than everything, distinct from it, the witness of the eye, the witness of the ear.

He is the witness of speech, the witness of the mind, the witness of the intellect, the witness of the vital breath, the witness of darkness, and the witness of all. Therefore, He is changeless, the Great Consciousness, dearer than all this, a mass of bliss. Indeed, thus He shines forth clearly before all this as the one essence—Brahman alone, which is undecaying, immortal, and fearless. Having attained Him, one should unify this four-footed [Brahman] with the measures and with the syllable *Oṃ*. The waking-state locus, the fourfold self, Viśva, and Vaiśvānara—these four forms are indeed the fourfold *Oṃ* itself.

This letter *a*—by virtue of its forms as the gross, the subtle, the seed, and the witness—because of its pervasiveness, or because of being the beginning, or because of being gross, subtle, a seed, and a witness—verily attains all this; and he who knows thus becomes the beginning of all.

The Taijasa, who is Hiranyagarbha, has four forms and abides in the state of dream; he is indeed the letter *U*, which likewise has four forms. For this letter *U* consists of the gross, the subtle, the seed, and the witness—by virtue of its forms as *U*. Because of excellence, because of being both, because of grossness, because of subtlety, because of being the seed, and because of being the witness, it indeed elevates the continuity of knowledge. And he who knows this becomes equal [to all].

The state of deep sleep has four aspects: the wise one (prājña) and the Lord (īśvara), which constitute its fourfold form. Indeed, this letter *M* is fourfold; for it consists of the gross, the subtle, the seed, and the witness—all of which are forms of *M*. Because of measuring (*miti*) and because of merging (*apīti*), and because of being gross, subtle, a seed, and a witness, he who knows thus indeed measures all this and becomes the one into whom all merges.

One should make the measures, the sub-measures, and the counter-measures; then the fourth is the "Devourer by the Lord" (*īśvaragrāsa*). He is self-ruling, himself the Lord, self-luminous, and fourfold in nature through the states of the Pervader (*ota*), the Permitter (*anujñātṛ*), and the Indifferent (*anujñāvikalpa*). For this Self is indeed the Pervader; for at the time of the end, he is the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) who, like the rays of the sun, permits all this. For this Self is the Permitter; he gives his own self to all this, making all this his very own self, just as darkness [is consumed]. This Self is indeed the Indifferent, whose essence is consciousness, just as [fire consumes] that which is to be burned.

Having burned [the fuel], this fire is indeed free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*); for, being beyond the reach of speech and mind, it is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). This fourfold *Oṃkāra* is indeed fourfold through the forms of *Oṃkāra*: as the Pervader (*ota*), the Permitter (*anujñātṛ*), and the Non-conceptual (*anujñā-vikalpa*). For all this is of the nature of name and form; yet, because it is the Fourth (*turīya*), because it is of the nature of consciousness, because it is the Pervader, the Permitter, and the Non-conceptual, all this is indeed non-conceptual in form. Indeed, there is no differentiation whatsoever therein. Now, its instruction is this: the fourth state, which is beyond the measures (*mātra*) and is not subject to worldly transaction (*avyavahārya*).

The cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is auspicious non-duality; the syllable *Oṃ* is the Self itself. He who knows this enters the Self by means of the Self. This hero, by means of the Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh, the king of mantras, should know the Fourth (*turīya*). For he illuminates the Self: capable of destroying everything, unable to be overcome, the Lord, all-pervading, eternally radiant, devoid of ignorance and its effects, the remover of the bondage of one's own self, always free from duality, whose nature is bliss, the substratum of all, pure existence (*sanmātra*), with the darkness of ignorance and delusion dispelled—“I am indeed that.”
Therefore, one should contemplate this very Self as the Supreme Brahman, thinking: "This is indeed the Hero, Nṛsiṃha. Thus ends the second section. 2.

Of that very *praṇava*, its first *mātrā* becomes the first foot (*pāda*), the second [the second], and the third [the third]; the fourth consists of the permission (*anujñā*), the one who grants permission (*anujñātṛ*), and the form of their differentiation (*vikalpa*). Having sought out the fourfold Fourth (*turīya*) by means of that [fourth *mātrā*] and with the fourth foot, one should swallow it while contemplating it with that fourth [state]. Of this very *praṇava*, its first *mātrā* is the earth, the syllable *a*; it is the *Ṛgveda* through the *ṛc*s, Brahmā, the Vasus, the *Gāyatrī* meter, and the Gārhapatya fire; that is the first foot.

And in all the quarters, it is fourfold by way of the gross, the subtle, the seed, and the witness. The second quarter is the intermediate space; that is the letter *U*. It consists of the *Yajus* formulas, the Yajurveda, Viṣṇu, the Rudras, the Triṣṭubh meter, and the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. That is the second quarter, and it is fourfold in all the quarters by way of the gross, the subtle, the seed, and the witness. The third quarter is heaven; that is the letter *M*. It consists of the Sāman chants, the Sāmaveda, the Rudras and Ādityas, the Jagatī meter, and the Āhavanīya fire. That is the third quarter, and it is fourfold in all the quarters.

The fourfold Self consists of the gross, the subtle, the seed, and the witness. At the conclusion of this [Oṃ], there is the half-measure of the fourth; that is the world of Soma, the syllable Oṃ, the Atharva-veda with its Atharvaṇa mantras, the Saṃvartaka fire, the Maruts, the Virāj, the Single Seer (Ekārṣi), and she is remembered as the Radiant One (Bhāsvatī). This constitutes the fourth quarter. And in all the quarters, the fourfold Self exists through the gross, subtle, seed, and witness aspects. Having made each measure, sub-measure, and counter-measure [of the syllable] consist of the forms of the Permitted, the Permission-giver, and the Indefinite (the Witness), the Knower—having offered his consciousness as an oblation—should swallow [all duality] while meditating. Thus he becomes immortal.

Pure, seated, and free from agitation, having experienced this in this well-regulated discipline and having seen all this here, he—being devoid of phenomenal expansion (prapañca), yet complete, possessing a support, consisting of nectar, and fourfold in nature—should then unite that very one, who is sevenfold and fourfold in nature, with the Root-Fire (mūlāgni) in the form of fire as the Praṇava, at the Great Seat (mahāpīṭha) along with his retinue; and he should unite the sevenfold and fourfold *a* (the letter *a*), which is Rudra, with the sevenfold, fourfold, and seventy-four-fold *oṃ*, the Lord of All, at the center of the eyebrows.

At the *dvādaśānta*, one should worship the sevenfold self, the fourfold self, and the forty-ninefold self—the *Oṃkāra* which is the fourth state (*turya*) and consists of the nectar of bliss—with the nectar of bliss at the *ṣoḍaśānta*. Having thus worshipped these fourfold [aspects], as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—both as the three distinct [deities] and as the three undivided, and likewise in the form of the *liṅga*—one should worship them with fourfold offerings. Then, withdrawing [the deity] from the *liṅga* by means of its splendor, one should pervade the three bodies with that light, inflame the Self which is their substratum, and [merge] that splendor...

Having taken hold of the power whose nature is one's own consciousness, having achieved unity with the qualities (guṇas), and having withdrawn the gross into the subtle, and the subtle into the causal, one should swallow [the object] while contemplating it in its form as the measured (mātrā) consisting of the "impulse" (otā), the "permission" (anujñā), and the "indeterminate" (anujñāvikalpa). Thus ends the third section. 3.

Having bowed to that very Self, the supreme Brahman, the syllable Om, which shines at the tip of the fourth Om, with the Anuṣṭubh verse and having propitiated it, one should withdraw [the mind] with "Om" and then contemplate it as "I. Then, having bowed to this very Self, the supreme Brahman, the syllable Om, which shines at the tip of the fourth Om, as the eleven-fold Nṛsiṃha, and withdrawing [the mind] with "Om," one should contemplate it. Then, having contemplated this very Self, the supreme Brahman, the syllable Om, which shines at the tip of the fourth Om, by means of the Praṇava, one should bow to it with the Anuṣṭubh verse.

Having contemplated the Supreme Brahman—the Self that is full of Being-Consciousness-Bliss—as the ninefold Being-Consciousness-Bliss-full Self within the selves that are full of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, one should take up the self as "I" and, by means of the mind, unify it with Brahman. Indeed, it is by means of the Anuṣṭubh [meter] that he fasts; for he, being the Self of all, everywhere, and at all times, eats everything—this Nṛsiṃha is the Supreme Lord, for he, being the Self of all, everywhere, and at all times, eats everything. This Nṛsiṃha alone is the One, He is the Fourth (Turiya), He is the Fierce (Ugra), He is the Hero (Vīra), He is the Great (Mahān), He is indeed this very one.

"This is Viṣṇu; this very one is the blazing one; this very one has faces on all sides; this is Nṛsiṃha; this very one is the Terrifying (Bhīṣaṇa); this very one is the Auspicious (Bhadra); this very one is the Death of Death; this very one I bow to; this very one am I. Thus, having ascended yoga, one should fix the Anuṣṭubh verse upon Brahman as the syllable Om. Regarding this, there are these two verses: "Having steadied the lion, having yoked his own sons who seek qualities, having struck with the horns of the bull, having subdued and crushed the quivering, wicked woman, and having devoured her with the lion—this is that Hero."

Having touched the feet protruding from the horn and having killed them, he himself devoured them; and having bowed down many times and gazed upon him, Nṛsiṃha himself arose. Thus ends the fourth section. 4.

Now, this very syllable *A* has the meaning of being most fully attained (*āptatama*); it resides in the Self, in the divine Nṛsiṃha, in Brahman. For he alone is most fully attained; for he is the witness; for he is the Lord; for he is all-pervading; for this entire universe is not [other than] him; for he is the most pervasive; for this entire universe is that which is the Self, which is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*). He alone is the Fierce One (*ugra*), for he is the most pervasive; he alone is the Hero (*vīra*), for he is the most pervasive; he alone is the Great One (*mahān*), for he is the most pervasive; he alone is Viṣṇu, for he is the most pervasive; he alone is the Blazing One (*jvalan*), for he is the most pervasive.

This indeed is Sarvatomukha (the one facing all directions), for he is the most pervasive; this indeed is Nṛsiṃha (the Man-Lion), for he is the most pervasive; this indeed is Bhīṣaṇa (the Terrifying), for he is the most pervasive; this indeed is Bhadra (the Auspicious), for he is the most pervasive; this indeed is Mṛtyumṛtyu (the Death of Death), for he is the most pervasive; this indeed I bow to, for he is the most pervasive; this indeed am I, for he is the most pervasive. He who knows thus—that the Self alone is the god Nṛsiṃha, who is Brahman—becomes that. He is free from desire, devoid of desire, his desires fulfilled, with the Self as his sole desire. His vital breaths...

Departing from here, they are absorbed right here; being Brahman, one attains Brahman. Now, this very syllable *Oṃ*—whose meaning is the most exalted—resides in the God Nṛsiṃha, who is the Self and Brahman. Therefore, He is the true essence; for there is nothing else that is immeasurable or not self-luminous. He is indeed self-luminous, unattached, and beholds nothing else. Since the Self is thus, there is no other way of attainment, for this alone is the supreme, the Self-only. He alone is Ugra, for He alone is the most exalted; He alone is Viṣṇu, for He alone is the most exalted; He alone is...

For this one is indeed the Blazing One; he is the Supreme; he is the All-facing One; he is indeed the Supreme; he is the Man-lion (Nṛsiṃha); he is indeed the Supreme; he is the Terrifying One; he is indeed the Supreme; he is the Auspicious One; he is indeed the Supreme; he is the Death of Death; he is indeed the Supreme; he is the One I bow to; he is indeed the Supreme; he is indeed I; he is indeed the Supreme. Therefore, one should know him as the Self alone. He who knows thus becomes the Self, the God Nṛsiṃha, Brahman. He is free from desire, devoid of desire, his desires fulfilled.

One who desires the Self—his vital breaths do not depart; they dissolve right here. Being Brahman, he attains Brahman. Now, this very syllable *Makāra* signifies great majesty (*mahāvibhūti*); it resides in the Lord Nṛsiṃha himself, in Brahman. Therefore, He is not limited, He is of diverse forms, self-luminous, Brahman itself, the most attained, the most excellent. This very one is Brahman, the omniscient, possessed of great *māyā*, and of great majesty. This very one is the Fierce (*ugra*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Hero (*vīra*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is... [the Terrible (*ghora*)], for He possesses great majesty; this very one is... [the Terrible (*bhīma*)], for He possesses great majesty. This very one is the Great (*mahat*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Pervasive (*vyāpaka*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unchanging (*avyaya*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Imperishable (*akṣara*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Support (*dhṛti*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Truth (*satya*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Auspicious (*śiva*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Bliss (*sukha*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Tranquil (*śānta*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Infinite (*ananta*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the All-pervading (*sarvagata*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the All (*sarva*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Supreme (*para*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Undecaying (*ajara*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Deathless (*amṛta*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Fearless (*abhaya*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Non-dual (*advaita*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the One-without-a-second (*advitīya*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Stainless (*nirañjana*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Pure (*viśuddha*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unborn (*aja*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unborn (*ajāta*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Uncreated (*akṛta*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unstruck (*atāḍita*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unperceivable (*agrāhya*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unnameable (*anāmaka*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unthinkable (*acintya*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unknowable (*avijñeya*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unmanifest (*alakṣaṇa*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unmoving (*acala*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unshakable (*akampa*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unfathomable (*agādha*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unmeasurable (*ameya*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Ungraspable (*agrāhya*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unobtainable (*alabhyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unconquerable (*ajeyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unassailable (*adharṣyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unvanquishable (*anirjityatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unconquerable (*asādhyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unapproachable (*agamyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unattainable (*aprāpyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unconceivable (*acintyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unmanifest (*apratarkyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unknowable (*avijñeyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unseen (*adṛṣṭatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unheard (*aśrutatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unperceived (*amatatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unreached (*avijñātatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unborn (*ajanmatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unoriginated (*anutpādatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Uncaused (*ahetutama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unproduced (*akāryatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Uncreated (*akṛtatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unstruck (*atāḍitatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unperceivable (*agrāhyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unnameable (*anāmakatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unthinkable (*acintyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unknowable (*avijñeyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unmanifest (*alakṣaṇatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unmoving (*acalatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unshakable (*akampatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unfathomable (*agādhatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unmeasurable (*ameyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Ungraspable (*agrāhyatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unobtainable (*alabhyatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unconquerable (*ajeyatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unassailable (*adharṣyatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unvanquishable (*anirjityatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unconquerable (*asādhyatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unapproachable (*agamyatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unattainable (*aprāpyatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unconceivable (*acintyatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unmanifest (*apratarkyatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unknowable (*avijñeyatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unseen (*adṛṣṭatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unheard (*aśrutatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unperceived (*amatatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unreached (*avijñātatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unborn (*ajanmatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unoriginated (*anutpādatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Uncaused (*ahetutatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Unproduced (*akāryatamatama*), for He possesses great majesty; this very one is the Uncreated (*akṛ

For this indeed is the Great One with great majesty; this alone is Viṣṇu with great majesty; this indeed is the Blazing One with great majesty; this alone is the All-facing One with great majesty; this indeed is Nṛsiṃha with great majesty; this alone is the Terrifying One with great majesty; this indeed is the Auspicious One with great majesty; this alone is the Death of Death with great majesty; this indeed I bow to with great majesty; this alone am I with great majesty.

Therefore, by means of the syllables *a* and *u*, one should seek this Self—the most trustworthy, the most excellent, pure consciousness alone, the seer of all, the witness of all, the devourer of all, the object of all love, consisting solely of existence-consciousness-bliss, the single flavor that shines forth clearly before all this—by means of the syllable *m*, one should know it as the Supreme Brahman, the Great Illusion, the Great Glory, consisting solely of existence-consciousness-bliss, the single flavor, the very Citadel. He who knows thus becomes the Lord Nṛsiṃha, the Self, which is indeed the Supreme Brahman.

He is without desire, free from desire, one whose desires are fulfilled, one whose desire is the Self; his vital breaths do not depart, but are absorbed right here. Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman—thus spoke Prajāpati, thus spoke Prajāpati. Thus ends the fifth section. 5.

Those gods desired to know this Self, but the demonic evil seized them. They reflected: "Come, let us devour this demonic evil. Thus, they [devoured] that very Self—the fourth of the fourth—which is illumined at the peak of the syllable *oṃ*; which is fierce yet non-fierce, a hero yet non-heroic, great yet non-great, Viṣṇu yet non-Viṣṇu, blazing yet non-blazing, facing all directions yet not facing all directions; who is the Man-Lion yet not the Man-Lion, terrifying yet non-terrifying, auspicious yet non-auspicious, the death of death yet the deathless death.

"I bow; I do not bow; I am not; I am not"—by means of this *Nṛsiṃha-anuṣṭubh* alone did they awaken. To them, that demonic evil became the light of the mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānandaghanajyoti*). Therefore, one whose impurities are not yet ripened should know this very Self—the fourth of the fourth (*turīyaturīya*)—which is illuminated at the peak of the syllable *Oṃ*, by means of this *Nṛsiṃha-anuṣṭubh* alone; for him, the demonic evil becomes the light of the mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss. Those gods, desiring to transcend that light and perceiving fear in the second [state], [perceived] this very [Self] illuminated at the peak of the syllable *Oṃ*.

Having sought the Self, which is the fourth of the fourth, by means of the *anuṣṭubh* verse and having become established in It by means of the *praṇava*, that light of theirs—which is before all this, well-shining yet non-manifest, non-dual, inconceivable, signless, self-luminous, a mass of bliss, and void—became manifest. One who knows thus becomes the supreme Brahman itself, which is self-luminous. Those gods, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, along with their means, became formless, without possessions, without tufts of hair, and without sacred threads.

Blind, deaf, deluded, impotent, mute, wandering like madmen—yet peaceful, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, composed, delighting in the Self, sporting with the Self, coupling with the Self, and finding bliss in the Self; knowing the *praṇava* alone to be the supreme Brahman, the light of the Self, the Void, they find their ultimate fulfillment therein. Therefore, performing the vow of the gods, one should come to rest in the *oṃkāra*, the supreme Brahman. He beholds the Self within himself as the supreme Brahman. Regarding this, there is this verse:

The gods indeed said to Prajāpati, "May the Blessed One explain this to us further. He replied, "So be it. [He explained: Because of his being unborn, immortal, ageless, deathless, free from sorrow, free from delusion, free from hunger, free from thirst, and non-dual, one should seek this Self through the syllable *oṃ*. And because of his being supreme (*utkṛṣṭatva*), his being the progenitor (*utpādakatva*), his being the one who enters (*utpraveṣṭatva*), his being the arouser (*utthāpayitṛtva*), his being the seer (*uddraṣṭṛtva*), his being the cutter (*utkartṛtva*), his being the warder-off of evil paths (*utpathavārakatva*), his being the devourer (*udgrāsatva*), his being the bewildered (*udbhrāntatva*), and his being transcendent over all transformations (*uttīrṇavikṛtatva*), one should seek this supreme Self through the syllable *oṃ*.

Having sought the Brahman-Nṛsiṃha through the syllable *A*, one draws this Self—the first half (*ā*)—and transforms it into a lion; then, having drawn that lion by means of the second half (*u*), one should unify it with this Self by means of the half-syllable *M*. This is because of its greatness, its majesty, its measurability, its liberation, its divinity, its sovereignty, its great being, its great consciousness, its great bliss, and its great lordship. He who knows this becomes self-ruling (*svarāj*), bodiless, without senses, without breath, beyond darkness, consisting solely of Being-Consciousness-Bliss. "Who are you? "I am the Self. Thus he says.

He said: "It is exactly thus; this whole universe is 'I' (Aham). Therefore, the name for everything begins with this letter 'A'. That very [letter] becomes all, for this Self is indeed within all. Indeed, this whole universe is not without the Self; 'I' (Aham) said this. This whole universe is indeed the Self alone. Therefore, by means of the letter 'A', which is the Self of all, one should seek the Self that is the Self of all. This whole universe is Brahman alone, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (Saccidānanda). This whole universe is of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss. For this whole universe is Being—Being, Being; and for this whole universe is Consciousness."

"It shines and it illuminates"—is this "Being" (sat)? "This is this, this is not"—is this experience? What is this? "This is this, this is not"—he spoke while experiencing through non-speaking alone. In this very same way, he spoke while experiencing consciousness (cit) and bliss (ānanda) through non-speaking alone, [saying] "everything else. This is the name of the Supreme Bliss, Brahman: "Brahman. Its final syllable is this letter *m*; that indeed becomes it. Therefore, one should seek the Supreme Brahman by means of the letter *m*. "What is this?"—"Thus" (*evam*)—he said; "thus" is the letter *u*. Without doubt, having sought this Self by means of the letter *a*, [one realizes it].

One should connect [the syllable] with *makāra* through Brahman; by means of *ukāra*, being free from doubt, one becomes bodiless, without senses, without breath, beyond darkness, consisting solely of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, and becomes self-sovereign—he who knows thus. Indeed, all this is Brahman, because of its being the Eater, its fierceness, its heroism, its greatness, its pervasiveness (*viṣṇutva*), its brilliance, its facing in all directions, its being the Man-Lion (*nṛsiṃhatva*), its terror, its auspiciousness, its being the Death of Death, its being the "I-not-I," and its being the "I-say. Thus it is constantly.

For this Brahman, because of its fierceness, heroism, greatness, pervasiveness (Viṣṇu-nature), brilliance, being all-facing, being the Man-Lion (Nṛsiṃha), its terrifying nature, its auspiciousness, its being the death of death, and its being the object of salutation—therefore, having sought the Supreme Brahman through the syllable *A*, one should seek with the syllable *Ma* that which protects the mind and so forth, the witness of the mind and so forth. When it perceives all this, then all this enters into it; when it awakens, then all this arises from it alone. Having thus withdrawn all that [into itself], it remains as that alone.

Having pushed back, crushed, incinerated, and consumed [all things], he gives himself alone; being exceedingly fierce, exceedingly heroic, exceedingly great—Viṣṇu, exceedingly blazing, exceeding all-faced, exceeding Nṛsiṃha, exceedingly terrifying, exceedingly auspicious, exceeding the death of death, exceedingly bowed-to, and exceedingly "I"—having become thus, he always abides in his own majesty. Therefore, one should unify him with the Supreme Brahman through the meaning of the syllable *A*; without doubt, by means of the syllable *U*, he becomes bodiless, devoid of senses, without breath, without mind, consisting solely of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, and he becomes self-ruling—he who knows thus.

Thus says the Veda. Regarding this, there is this verse: "Having drawn out a horn and half a horn, one should join it with this horn; one should join this horn to another horn, and that [other] with this as well. Thus ends the seventh section. 7.

Now, by the fourth [syllable], this Self, Nṛsiṃha, is woven across and woven lengthwise; for in Him is all, He is the Self of all, and indeed all is He. Therefore, He is non-dual, this Self is one alone, without differentiation. For there is no real object here; He is as if woven across, a mass of Being, a mass of Consciousness, a mass of Bliss, of one single essence, beyond all transactional usage by anyone, and without a second. Woven across and woven lengthwise is this very syllable *Oṃ*. When asked "Is it thus? or "Is it not thus?", He says simply "Om. The syllable *Oṃ* is speech, and speech indeed is all this; for there is nothing here that is without sound, consisting entirely of Consciousness.

This syllable *oṃ* is indeed this all, which consists of consciousness; therefore, the Supreme Lord alone is that one reality. This is composed of immortality; this is Brahman. He who knows this becomes Brahman, which is indeed fearless—this is the secret. For this Self is the authorizer (*anujñātṛ*), for it authorizes its own self as everything. Indeed, this whole world does not exist by itself apart from the Self-knower. This *oṃ* is neither an authorizer nor a non-authorizer, because of its being unattached, changeless, and non-existent [as a separate entity]. It is the authorizer of the other; for through *oṃ*, it authorizes. The syllable *oṃ* is speech.

Speech alone authorizes all this, for this *oṃkāra* consists of consciousness (*cit*); and consciousness indeed assimilates all this—which is devoid of self—into itself. Therefore, that which is the Supreme Lord alone becomes the one; this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman. Verily, Brahman is fearless; verily, he who knows thus becomes Brahman, which is fearless. This is the secret: for this Self has the single flavor of authorization (*anujñā*); it is a mass of pure intelligence (*prajñānaghana*) because it shines forth clearly before everything. Therefore, it is a mass of consciousness alone; for it is neither the one who authorizes nor the one being authorized. This is its true nature (*ātmya*).

Indeed, all this is of the single flavor of permission (*anujñā*). This syllable *Oṃ* is indeed permission; for it is through "Om" that one grants permission. *Oṃ* is speech, for it is through speech that one grants permission. This *Oṃ* is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), for consciousness alone is the one who grants permission. Therefore, that Supreme Lord alone becomes this One. This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman. Indeed, Brahman is fearless; he who knows thus becomes fearless—this is the secret. For this Self is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*) because of its non-duality; this *Oṃ* is free from conceptual construction because of its very non-duality, and it is composed of consciousness for that same reason.

This is indeed the syllable Om; therefore, it is the Supreme Lord alone, for that becomes one and undifferentiated. There is no division whatsoever here, nor is there any division at all therein. For he who perceives division as if it were real is split a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and goes from death to death. This is non-dual, self-luminous, the Great Bliss, the Self, the Immortal, the Fearless—this is Brahman. Verily, Brahman is fearless; verily, one becomes fearless Brahman who knows this. This is the secret.
Thus ends the eighth section. ||8||

The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, teach us this very OṂkāra as our Self. He replied, "So be it. This Self is the witness, the assenter; it is Nṛsiṃha, whose nature is consciousness alone, for it is perceived as changeless, in all things and everywhere. Indeed, there is no establishment of duality; the Self alone is established as non-dual. For by means of Māyā, it appears as if something else. That indeed is this Self, the Supreme; this alone is everything. For thus, through wisdom, this entire world is the Self, the Supreme Self alone.

Although self-luminous, because it is not an object of cognition, it knows itself while not knowing anything else; for such is the nature of experience. And Māyā, which is of the nature of darkness, is that experience; it is insentient, delusive in essence, and infinite. It is the manifester of this form (the world), and though eternally ceased, it is seen by the deluded as if it were the Self itself. Through its presence and absence, it displays existence and non-existence, and through its independence and dependence, it manifests sovereignty and lack thereof. This very [Māyā] possesses manifold potencies, like the generality of a banyan seed; just as, for example:

Just as a single banyan seed, having produced many banyan trees along with their seeds that are not distinct from itself, remains fully present within each of them; even so, this Māyā, having manifested fields that are full and non-distinct from itself, brings about the appearance of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). She herself becomes both Māyā and Avidyā. This Māyā is variegated, very firm, and possesses many sprouts; she is herself differentiated by the qualities (guṇas), and even within the sprouts differentiated by the qualities, she exists everywhere in the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, illumined by consciousness. Therefore, [all this arises] from the Self alone.

The threefold nature exists everywhere: the source, the individual soul who identifies with it, and the Lord who governs it. Hiranyagarbha, possessing all forms of egoity, is the Lord in his threefold aspect, his consciousness being manifest like that of the Supreme Lord; for this Lord is omnipresent, consisting of action and knowledge, and everything is composed of Him. All individual souls consist of everything in all their states, yet they remain limited. Indeed, He, having created the elements, the senses, the Viraj, the deities, and the sheaths, entered them; though Himself uninfatuated, He remains as if infatuated, conducting worldly affairs through Māyā alone. Therefore, He is non-dual.

Thus, this Self is pure existence (*sanmātra*), eternal, pure, awakened, true, liberated, stainless, all-pervading, non-dual bliss, the supreme, the one essence of the inner witness, known through these means of valid cognition. For all this is mere existence; indeed, Brahman alone was established as "Being" even before [creation]. Nothing whatsoever is experienced here, nor is there the experience of ignorance. In that which is self-luminous, the witness of all, changeless, and non-dual, one sees here too only pure existence; everything else is unreal. Truly, it has been thus established from the beginning as being without origin.

Established within its own self as a mass of blissful consciousness, it is both accomplished and unaccomplished; it is Viṣṇu, Īśāna, Brahmā, and everything else. Because it is all-pervading, it is therefore everything. Thus the Self is pure, of an inviolable nature, awakened, and of the nature of happiness. Indeed, this world is not soulless, nor is the Self something other than what is established before us. For this entire universe is never apart from the Self. The Self, established in its own majesty, independent, one alone, the witness, and self-luminous—what is that? It is the eternal Self. Have no doubt about this; for it is this very Self that accomplishes all this.

The Seer is the witness of the seer, changeless, established, and faultless; through the observation of both the external and internal, he is most clearly manifest. He is beyond the state of being seen or unseen, beyond all worldly transaction, neither small nor not small, the specific witness, non-different, free from pleasure and pain, non-dual, the Supreme Self, omniscient, infinite, undivided, and non-dual. Consciousness is always present through Māyā, for there is no lack of consciousness in that which is self-luminous. "Are you yourselves not seen? Is there indeed no second? Are you yourselves [the truth]? Speak, O Blessed One!"—thus spoke the gods.

[The Teacher] said: "If you alone are seen, then you are not knowers of the Self; for this Self is indeed unattached. Therefore, you yourselves are self-luminous. They replied: "This is indeed so, because we consist of existence and consciousness; therefore, it is you alone [who are the Self]. He said: "No, it is not so. They said: "Then who are we? He said: "How do you see? They said: "We do not know. Then he said: "Therefore, you yourselves are self-luminous, yet you do not consist of existence and consciousness. For these two [the Self and the world] were previously well-illuminated, beyond all transactional usage, non-dual, known as the Unknown. This is not known as an object of cognition, for it is beyond both the known and the unknown. Thus they spoke. He [the Teacher] remained silent.

He said: "This indeed is that non-dual Brahman—because it is Brahman, it is eternal, pure, awakened, liberated, true, subtle, all-pervading, non-dual, and consisting solely of existence, bliss, and consciousness; it is the Self itself, beyond all worldly transaction by any means. Therefore, seeing this very Self as 'Om,' behold it! This is the Truth: the Self is indeed Brahman, and Brahman is indeed the Self. Regarding this, there should be no doubt at all. Om, the Truth! Only the wise perceive this."

For they behold this which is soundless, touchless, formless, tasteless, scentless, inexpressible, not to be given, not to be gone to, not to be released, not to be gladdened, not to be thought, not to be understood, not to be made the ego, not to be perceived, not to be made to breathe in, not to be made to breathe out, not to be made to circulate through the body, not to be made to rise, not to be made to equalize; which is beyond the senses, beyond objects, without instruments, without marks, unattached, devoid of qualities, changeless, indefinable, without being, without passion, without darkness, without illusion, and fearless.

"Behold that which is revealed by the Upanishads, which is brilliantly shining, which shines all at once, which is brilliantly shining before all this, and which is non-dual—'I am He, the Swan'. He said: "Has this been seen, or has it not been seen? They replied: "It has been seen; it is beyond the known and the unknown. They asked: "Where is this? How is it? They replied: "What is there to be gained from that? Nothing at all. He said: "You yourselves are of a wondrous nature. They said: "No. He said: "Then say 'Yes,' grant permission, and speak of Him. They replied: "He is both known and unknown," and they said: "But not as such. Thus it was said.

"Speak thus," he said, "that it is established by itself. [The gods] replied, "We see it indeed, O Venerable One; yet we do not see it, nor are we able to speak of it. Homage to you, O Venerable One; be gracious. He said, "Do not fear; ask. They asked, "Where is this permission? He said, "This very Self is that. They said, "Homage to you; we are yours. Thus Prajāpati instructed the gods, instructing them again and again. Regarding this, there is this verse: "One should know the woven through the woven, the inner one who grants permission. Having obtained the non-dual permission, one should approach the witness. Thus ends the ninth section. 9.

Oṃ. May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones. With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise [you] and attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods. Oṃ. May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel is uninjured, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us. Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace! Thus ends the Nṛsiṃhottaratāpinī Upaniṣad.
